purpose: Independent smoke-test evaluation of Phase 4 Lesson Reconciliation quality. No prior scores are included.

lesson.title: Outras técnicas Word Embedding: TF, TF-IDF e LSA
lesson.description: Ao longo deste encontro, outras técnicas de Word Embedding serão apresentadas as pessoas desenvolvedoras. Assim, o objetivo desta abordagem é que elas possam comparar as técnicas que foram apresentadas e verificar que cada uma delas possui um tipo de aplicação característica para sua aplicação.
related_labels: Semântica da sentença e conhecimento do ambiente (Análise semântica)

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word embeddings are numerical representations of text for machine learning
before_phase4_candidates.description: Word embeddings are dense vector representations that encode semantic meaning, allowing NLP models to process text as numbers.
coverage_criteria: Student can state what word embeddings are and why numerical representations are needed.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video introduces word embeddings as mathematical representations of text necessary for ML models.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational definition that sets the stage for all subsequent topics; it is narrow enough to be checked with a single recall question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: One-hot encoding creates sparse, vocabulary-sized vectors
before_phase4_candidates.description: One-hot encoding represents each word as a vector with a single 1 at the word's vocabulary index and 0s elsewhere, resulting in high-dimensional sparse vectors.
coverage_criteria: Student can create a one-hot vector for a given word from a small vocabulary.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video uses a concrete example to illustrate how one-hot encoding works for a simple vocabulary.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific encoding technique; the concept is small enough to be checked by asking the student to produce a one-hot vector.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Count-based text representations such as Bag-of-Words, N-gram, and TF-IDF
before_phase4_candidates.description: Bag-of-Words counts word occurrences ignoring order; N-gram counts sequences of n words; TF-IDF weights term frequency by inverse document frequency to highlight important words.
coverage_criteria: Student can compute Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF vectors for a small corpus.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly covers Bag-of-Words, N-gram, and TF-IDF as count-based techniques, with on-screen formulas and examples.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Grouping these three together as 'count-based methods' creates a teachable block that contrasts with later embedding approaches; it is checkable with a few computation tasks.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Shortcomings of count-based methods: no context, unknown words, sparse vectors
before_phase4_candidates.description: Count-based methods ignore word context, cannot handle words not seen during training, and produce sparse vectors, which are computationally inefficient.
coverage_criteria: Student can list at least two limitations of count-based representations.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video enumerates these three shortcomings explicitly as motivation for embeddings.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a focused list that directly transitions to the need for dense embeddings; its small size makes it easy to verify.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Embeddings use dense vectors with fewer dimensions than the vocabulary
before_phase4_candidates.description: Unlike one-hot encoding, word embeddings are dense vectors where most elements are non-zero, and the vector dimension is typically much smaller than the vocabulary size.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain the difference between dense and sparse vectors.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video defines a dense vector and contrasts it with sparse representations right after introducing embeddings.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This specific property of embeddings is a core checkable fact that supports understanding of embedding efficiency.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word similarity is defined by shared contexts, not spelling
before_phase4_candidates.description: Words like 'tea' and 'coffee' are considered similar because they appear with words like 'breakfast' or 'drink', while 'tea' and 'pea' are not similar despite similar spelling.
coverage_criteria: Student can give an example of two contextually similar words and explain why they are similar.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video uses the 'tea/coffee' vs 'tea/pea' example to illustrate distributional similarity.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept is small enough to check by asking for a definition and an original example.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Embedding space places words so that distance indicates similarity
before_phase4_candidates.description: In a multidimensional embedding space, the Euclidean or cosine distance between word vectors measures their semantic similarity; smaller distance means more similar.
coverage_criteria: Student can interpret a 2D embedding plot and identify which words are most similar.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video shows 1D and 2D examples with distance calculations between 'tea', 'coffee', and 'pea'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a single, testable concept about the geometric interpretation of embeddings.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Ideal embeddings cluster similar words and support analogies
before_phase4_candidates.description: In a well-trained embedding space, similar words group together (e.g., 'king', 'queen', 'sovereign') and vector arithmetic captures analogical relations like 'king - man + woman = queen'.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain the analogy property and give an example.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly states clustering and analogy properties as characteristics of an ideal embedding space.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a higher-level property still checkable with a single analogy task.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Custom embedding layer trained as part of a model
before_phase4_candidates.description: A neural network can include an embedding layer that is initialized randomly and trained end-to-end for a specific task, producing specialized word representations, but requiring large data.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe how a custom embedding layer is trained within a model.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video presents the custom embedding layer as the first method for creating embeddings, with a diagram including the Transformer architecture.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This method is distinct enough from other training approaches to stand alone and be checked with a simple explanation.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word2vec: CBOW and Skip-gram architectures
before_phase4_candidates.description: Word2vec learns word embeddings by predicting a target word from context (CBOW) or context words from a target word (Skip-gram) using a single-layer neural network.
coverage_criteria: Student can differentiate CBOW and Skip-gram and state which predicts what.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explains the two Word2vec variants with architecture diagrams and describes their prediction goals.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a core embedding technique checkable by comparing the two sub-architectures.

before_phase4_candidates.label: GloVe combines local and global context via co-occurrence matrices
before_phase4_candidates.description: GloVe extends Word2vec by training on a word co-occurrence matrix so that the dot product of word vectors approximates the log of their co-occurrence probability.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain how GloVe differs from Word2vec regarding global information.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video states GloVe adds global context to Word2vec and shows the co-occurrence matrix and training equation.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific enhancement of Word2vec, checkable by asking for the key difference.

before_phase4_candidates.label: fastText uses subword n-grams to handle rare and unknown words
before_phase4_candidates.description: fastText represents each word as the sum of its character n-gram embeddings, enabling it to handle out-of-vocabulary words and morphologically rich languages.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain how fastText's subword approach solves the out-of-vocabulary problem.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video describes fastText's subword training with an example and highlights its benefits for rare words.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a focused technique that can be checked by asking how it handles an unseen word.

before_phase4_candidates.label: ELMo produces dynamic, context-dependent word representations
before_phase4_candidates.description: ELMo uses a bidirectional LSTM to create word vectors that are functions of the entire input sentence, allowing it to distinguish homonyms like 'fair' in different contexts.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe how ELMo provides different embeddings for the same word in different sentences.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video highlights ELMo's context-dependence with the 'fair' example and shows its architecture.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a distinct approach to word representation, checkable by comparing static vs. dynamic embeddings.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Pre-trained embeddings can be used statically or fine-tuned
before_phase4_candidates.description: Pre-trained word vectors can be used as fixed features (static) or updated during task-specific training (fine-tuning) to adapt to the domain.
coverage_criteria: Student can list the two ways of using pre-trained embeddings and give a scenario for each.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video clearly states the two modes of using pre-trained embeddings in a dedicated section.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This practical decision point is checkable with a simple comparison question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Gensim library provides pre-trained word embeddings and similarity operations
before_phase4_candidates.description: Gensim offers downloadable pre-trained models (Word2vec, GloVe, fastText) and functions like most_similar() and distance() to explore semantic relationships and analogies.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code to load a pre-trained model from Gensim and find similar words.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates the Gensim library with code snippets for loading models and running similarity and analogy queries.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical tool concept that can be assessed by asking for a code snippet.

before_phase4_candidates.label: TF-IDF as a measure of word relevance
before_phase4_candidates.description: TF-IDF is a statistical measurement that evaluates how relevant a word is to a document in a collection of documents, commonly used in text analysis and NLP.
coverage_criteria: Explain what TF-IDF measures in a document corpus.
Describe the two components that make up TF-IDF.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Calculate TF-IDF in NLP (Simple Example)

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video introduces TF-IDF as a popular text representation, defines it as the product of TF and IDF, and summarizes its purpose and applications.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept encapsulates the core idea of TF-IDF and is checkable with basic recall questions, while allowing deeper understanding to be assessed by elaborating on its components.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Term Frequency (TF) calculation
before_phase4_candidates.description: Term Frequency is the frequency of a term in a specific document, often computed as the raw count divided by total words in that document.
coverage_criteria: Given a document and a term, compute the term frequency.
State that TF is specific to a single document.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Calculate TF-IDF in NLP (Simple Example)

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly defines TF and walks through a worked example calculating TF('fox', d1)=2/12 and TF('fox', d2)=3/12.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: TF is a fundamental building block of TF-IDF and is small enough to be verified with a simple arithmetic exercise.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) calculation
before_phase4_candidates.description: IDF is a corpus-level constant that measures how informative a term is, based on the log ratio of total documents to documents containing the term.
coverage_criteria: Given a corpus and a term, compute the IDF.
Explain why IDF equals zero when a term appears in every document.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Calculate TF-IDF in NLP (Simple Example)

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video defines IDF and provides the formula log(N/df), then calculates IDF('fox', D)=log(2/2)=0, illustrating that a term in all documents gets zero IDF.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: IDF is a key concept that can be checked by asking the student to compute it for a simple corpus or interpret the result.

before_phase4_candidates.label: TF-IDF computation as product of TF and IDF
before_phase4_candidates.description: The TF-IDF value for a term in a document is the product of its term frequency in that document and its inverse document frequency across the corpus.
coverage_criteria: Given TF(t,d) and IDF(t), calculate TFIDF(t,d).
Explain why a word with IDF=0 yields a TF-IDF of zero.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Calculate TF-IDF in NLP (Simple Example)

anchors.locator: 04:58 Solution: Calculating TF-IDF for each document

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video performs a step-by-step multiplication of TF and IDF values for the word 'fox' in two documents, showing TFIDF(d1)=0.17*0=0 and TFIDF(d2)=0.25*0=0.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is the operative core of TF-IDF and can be assessed by a single computation question, making it an appropriately sized candidate.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Preprocessing for Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF
before_phase4_candidates.description: Before computing TF and IDF in a bag-of-words model, text typically undergoes stemming and stop-word elimination to reduce noise and dimensionality.
coverage_criteria: List two common preprocessing steps used before TF-IDF calculation.
Explain why stemming and stop-word removal are beneficial.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Calculate TF-IDF in NLP (Simple Example)

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video mentions that systems using bag-of-words representation go through stemming and stop-word elimination before term counting, as shown in the diagram.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a supporting concept that can be checked with a short recall question, appropriate for a single candidate.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Document feature vectors from TF-IDF
before_phase4_candidates.description: After TF-IDF computation, each document becomes a feature vector, and the corpus is a set of such vectors, which can be used in data mining algorithms like classification, clustering, or retrieval.
coverage_criteria: Describe how a document is represented as a feature vector using TF-IDF.
Name at least two data mining tasks that can use such feature vectors.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Calculate TF-IDF in NLP (Simple Example)

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly states that each document becomes a feature vector and the corpus is a set of these feature vectors, which can be used in classification, clustering, or retrieval.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept bridges TF-IDF calculation to practical applications, and it can be verified by asking the student to explain the transformation or list tasks.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Applications of TF-IDF
before_phase4_candidates.description: TF-IDF is widely used in automated text analysis, scoring words for machine learning algorithms in NLP, document search, and information retrieval.
coverage_criteria: List at least three applications of TF-IDF.
Explain why TF-IDF is suitable for document search.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Calculate TF-IDF in NLP (Simple Example)

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video summarizes that TF-IDF has many uses, most importantly in automated text analysis, and is very useful for scoring words in ML algorithms for NLP, and was invented for document search and information retrieval.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This provides a high-level perspective on the value of TF-IDF and can be checked with recall of the applications mentioned in the source.

before_phase4_candidates.label: IDF zero and discriminative power
before_phase4_candidates.description: If a term appears in every document of the corpus, its IDF equals zero, resulting in a TF-IDF of zero and indicating the term is not discriminative.
coverage_criteria: Explain why a word that occurs in all documents gets a TF-IDF score of zero.
Interpret the meaning of a zero TF-IDF score for a term.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Calculate TF-IDF in NLP (Simple Example)

anchors.locator: 04:58 Solution: Calculating TF-IDF for each document

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The example calculates IDF('fox') = log(2/2) = 0, leading to TF-IDF = 0, and concludes that 'fox' is equally (equivalently zero) relevant to both documents, illustrating that such a term lacks discriminative power.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This insight reveals the intuitive justification for IDF and can be assessed with a single interpretation question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: TF-IDF: Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency
before_phase4_candidates.description: A numerical statistic that reflects the importance of a word to a document in a collection, computed as tf * idf, where tf is term frequency (count of term in document divided by document length) and idf is inverse document frequency (log(total documents / documents containing term)).
coverage_criteria: Student can write the TF-IDF formula and explain each component.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de texto TF-IDF

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The text defines tf-idf as tf * idf, explains tf as frequency/divided by document length, and idf as log(N/df) to diminish weight of common terms.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a key concept of the chapter, teachable as a single formula with components.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Comparison between Bag of Words and TF-IDF
before_phase4_candidates.description: Bag of words counts word occurrences without considering context or importance across documents. TF-IDF improves by weighting terms: frequent terms across many documents get lower weight, while rare but significant terms get higher weight.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain at least two differences between bag of words and TF-IDF.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de texto TF-IDF

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The text explicitly contrasts bag of words and TF-IDF, noting BOW's problem of highlighting frequent but irrelevant words, and TF-IDF's ability to adjust for term frequency across documents.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Understanding the distinction is crucial for choosing the right text representation method.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Using TfidfVectorizer from scikit-learn
before_phase4_candidates.description: The TfidfVectorizer class from sklearn.feature_extraction.text converts a collection of text documents into a TF-IDF feature matrix, with configurable parameters like stop_words, ngram_range, max_df, etc.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code that imports TfidfVectorizer, initializes it with stopwords, and applies fit_transform to a list of documents.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de texto TF-IDF

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The text provides an example using TfidfVectorizer, showing parameters and usage with Wikipedia data and stopwords.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical skill for applying TF-IDF in Python.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Stopword removal using NLTK
before_phase4_candidates.description: The nltk.corpus.stopwords module provides lists of common words to filter out during text preprocessing, which can be passed to TfidfVectorizer's stop_words parameter to ignore irrelevant terms.
coverage_criteria: Student can download stopwords for a language and use them in TfidfVectorizer.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de texto TF-IDF

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The example code uses stopwords from nltk to remove articles, prepositions, etc., improving TF-IDF results.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Stopword removal is a key preprocessing step that can be taught independently but is closely tied to TF-IDF implementation.

before_phase4_candidates.label: TF-IDF as a feature weighting scheme
before_phase4_candidates.description: TF-IDF produces a matrix where each document is represented by weighted terms. Terms with high TF-IDF scores are those that appear frequently in a specific document but rarely in the overall corpus, making them discriminative features.
coverage_criteria: Student can articulate why high TF-IDF terms are useful for distinguishing documents.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de texto TF-IDF

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source mentions that words repeating less have 'maior importância' (higher importance), indicating that TF-IDF highlights significant terms.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Understanding output interpretation is essential for using TF-IDF effectively.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Document representation as weighted term vectors
before_phase4_candidates.description: Each document is represented as a vector of TF-IDF weights for all terms in the vocabulary, allowing comparison using cosine similarity or other metrics.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that after TF-IDF, each document is a numerical vector.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de texto TF-IDF

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The text describes that TF-IDF provides a vector of characteristics for each document, and shows the resulting matrix.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational concept for text representation in NLP.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Preparing documents for TF-IDF: splitting text
before_phase4_candidates.description: To apply TF-IDF, text must be divided into individual documents (e.g., paragraphs, sentences). In the example, splitlines() breaks the Wikipedia content into paragraphs, each treated as a separate document.
coverage_criteria: Student can split a long text into logical units for TF-IDF processing.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de texto TF-IDF

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The code example uses splitlines() to split the Wikipedia page into paragraphs before feeding to TfidfVectorizer.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical step in preparing data for TF-IDF analysis.

before_phase4_candidates.label: TF-IDF formula components
before_phase4_candidates.description: Term frequency (tf) is the count of a term in a document normalized by document length. Inverse document frequency (idf) is log(total number of documents / number of documents containing the term). The product gives tf-idf.
coverage_criteria: Student can calculate tf and idf for a given term in a small corpus.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de texto TF-IDF

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The text provides the tf-idf formula and explains each part: tf is frequency divided by document length; idf uses log and document counts.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Understanding the formula is crucial for deeper use of TF-IDF.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Basic NLP Vocabulary: Document, Body, Dictionary, Topic
before_phase4_candidates.description: In NLP, a document is a collection of words representing a data instance; a body is the entire set of documents; a dictionary is the set of all words occurring in at least one document; a topic is a collection of co-occurring words.
coverage_criteria: Student can define document, body, dictionary, and topic in the context of natural language processing.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Introduction to Latent Semantic Analysis

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly defines these terms at the start to establish a common vocabulary for understanding LSA.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: These four terms are fundamental and small enough to be checked together in a single question asking for definitions.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) Defined
before_phase4_candidates.description: LSA is an unsupervised natural language processing technique that discovers hidden (latent) topics in text data and produces lower-dimensional representations of documents by encoding them in terms of these topics.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that LSA is an unsupervised technique for finding latent topics, and that it reduces dimensionality.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Introduction to Latent Semantic Analysis

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The section 'Understanding Latent Semantic Analysis' introduces LSA as an unsupervised technique targeting latent features and dimensionality reduction.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept captures the core definition of LSA in one teachable idea, appropriate for a single check-in question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Document-Term Matrix
before_phase4_candidates.description: A document-term matrix represents text documents as vectors in Euclidean space, where each row corresponds to a document and each column to a word from the dictionary, typically indicating presence (binary) or frequency.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe that a document-term matrix has rows for documents, columns for dictionary words, and cells indicating word occurrence.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Introduction to Latent Semantic Analysis

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explains the document-term matrix in detail, showing an example with four sentence fragments and binary values.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Focusing on the document-term matrix as a standalone concept allows checking understanding of this key representation method.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) for LSA
before_phase4_candidates.description: In LSA, Singular Value Decomposition is applied to the document-term matrix to reduce dimensionality and encode documents using latent features that represent topics, similar to Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
coverage_criteria: Student can state that SVD is used in LSA to reduce dimensionality and produce topic-based latent features, analogous to PCA.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Introduction to Latent Semantic Analysis

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video dedicates a section to SVD, explaining it as the second step of LSA that reduces dimensionality and encodes data with latent topics.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept isolates SVD's role in LSA, making it checkable with a question about its purpose and analogy to PCA.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Twitter Entity Sentiment Analysis Dataset
before_phase4_candidates.description: A Kaggle dataset containing multi-lingual tweets annotated with entity-level sentiment labels, intended for training and evaluating sentiment classification models.
coverage_criteria: Student can identify this dataset as a resource for entity-level sentiment analysis on tweets.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: ATIVIDADE: Estudo de caso - Aplicações de Análise de Sentimentos

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The entire source page describes this specific dataset.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Knowing about this dataset as a concrete resource is useful for practical projects and can be checked with a simple identification question.

reconciled_candidates.label: Word Embedding Fundamentals
reconciled_candidates.description: Word embeddings are dense numerical vectors that encode semantic meaning, allowing words to be compared by their context; similar words appear close in embedding space, and ideal embeddings should cluster synonyms and support vector analogies.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain why word embeddings are needed and state their key properties: dense vectors, context-based similarity, geometric distance, and the ideal of clustering and analogies.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates together define word embeddings, explain their core characteristics, and describe the desired properties of an embedding space, forming a single teachable concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: One-Hot Encoding
reconciled_candidates.description: One-hot encoding represents each word as a vector with a single 1 at its vocabulary index and zeros elsewhere, resulting in high-dimensional, sparse vectors.
coverage_criteria: Student can construct a one-hot vector for a given word from a small vocabulary and explain its limitations.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone basic technique distinct from dense and count-based representations.

reconciled_candidates.label: Count-Based Text Representations and Their Limitations
reconciled_candidates.description: Bag-of-words counts word occurrences, N-gram counts sequences, and TF-IDF weights terms by frequency and rarity. These methods produce sparse vectors, ignore word context, and fail on unseen words, motivating dense embeddings.
coverage_criteria: Student can compute a simple bag-of-words or TF-IDF vector and list at least two shortcomings of count-based methods.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: The description of count-based methods and the explicit list of shortcomings are logically connected, providing a complete motivation for embeddings.

reconciled_candidates.label: Custom Embedding Layer Training
reconciled_candidates.description: A neural network can include a trainable embedding layer that is initialized randomly and updated during task training, leading to specialized word representations but requiring large datasets.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe how a custom embedding layer is integrated into a model and when it might be preferred over pre-trained embeddings.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Distinct approach to obtaining word embeddings, separate from pre-trained models.

reconciled_candidates.label: Word2vec: CBOW and Skip-gram
reconciled_candidates.description: Word2vec learns static word embeddings by predicting a target word from context (CBOW) or context from a target (Skip-gram) using a simple neural network.
coverage_criteria: Student can differentiate CBOW and Skip-gram and explain their prediction objectives.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: A specific embedding technique taught as a standalone algorithm.

reconciled_candidates.label: GloVe: Global Vectors
reconciled_candidates.description: GloVe extends Word2vec by training on co-occurrence counts to incorporate global corpus statistics, where the dot product of vectors approximates log co-occurrence probability.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain how GloVe differs from Word2vec and why global context matters.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: A distinct enhancement of Word2vec that merits its own concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: fastText: Subword Embeddings
reconciled_candidates.description: fastText represents words as sums of character n-gram embeddings, allowing it to handle out-of-vocabulary words and morphological variants effectively.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain how fastText's subword approach solves the out-of-vocabulary problem and gives an example.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: A specific method with a unique approach not covered by other concepts.

reconciled_candidates.label: ELMo: Contextualized Word Representations
reconciled_candidates.description: ELMo generates dynamic, context-dependent embeddings using a bidirectional LSTM, so the same word can have different vectors in different sentences.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe how ELMo differs from static embeddings and why context matters for disambiguation.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: A paradigm shift from static to contextual embeddings, requiring a separate concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Using Pre-trained Word Embeddings
reconciled_candidates.description: Pre-trained embeddings can be used as fixed features (static) or fine-tuned on a task; the Gensim library provides convenient access to pre-trained models and similarity/analogy operations.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain when to use static vs fine-tuning and write a simple code snippet to load a Gensim model and find similar words.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Combines the conceptual decision of usage mode with a practical tool demonstration to form a complete teachable concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: TF-IDF: Core Computation
reconciled_candidates.description: TF-IDF measures word importance by multiplying term frequency (normalized count) and inverse document frequency (log ratio of total docs to docs containing the term); a term appearing in all documents gets IDF=0 and thus zero TF-IDF, indicating no discriminative power.
coverage_criteria: Student can compute TF, IDF, and TF-IDF for a term in a small document collection and interpret a zero TF-IDF score.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates overlap in teaching the TF-IDF definition, components, and step-by-step calculation; merging reduces redundancy into one clear lesson concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: TF-IDF Preprocessing and Vectorization
reconciled_candidates.description: Before TF-IDF, text is split into documents, stemmed, and stop-words are removed; then each document becomes a TF-IDF feature vector, forming a matrix of weighted terms suitable for machine learning.
coverage_criteria: Student can list preprocessing steps and explain how a document becomes a TF-IDF vector.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These steps together form the practical pipeline from raw text to TF-IDF representation.

reconciled_candidates.label: TF-IDF Applications and Comparison to Bag of Words
reconciled_candidates.description: TF-IDF improves on bag-of-words by down-weighting common terms, making it effective for information retrieval, document search, and text classification.
coverage_criteria: Student can name at least two applications of TF-IDF and explain why it is better than a simple bag-of-words.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates highlight the utility of TF-IDF and its advantages over BOW, providing a cohesive view.

reconciled_candidates.label: Implementing TF-IDF in Python with scikit-learn and NLTK
reconciled_candidates.description: Using the TfidfVectorizer class from scikit-learn to convert text documents into a TF-IDF feature matrix, including preprocessing with NLTK stopwords to filter out common words.
coverage_criteria: Student can write Python code to import TfidfVectorizer, load NLTK stopwords, initialize the vectorizer with stopwords, and fit_transform a list of text documents.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates provide complementary parts of a single practical pipeline: the vectorizer usage and stopword integration.

reconciled_candidates.label: LSA Introduction and NLP Key Terms
reconciled_candidates.description: Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) is an unsupervised NLP technique that discovers hidden topics and reduces dimensionality. Key terms: document (collection of words), body (set of documents), dictionary (set of unique words), topic (co-occurring words).
coverage_criteria: Student can define LSA and explain its purpose, and define the four key NLP terms (document, body, dictionary, topic) in the context of text analysis.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: The vocabulary definitions are introduced immediately before LSA in the source, and together they form the foundational knowledge for understanding LSA.

reconciled_candidates.label: LSA Steps: Document-Term Matrix and SVD
reconciled_candidates.description: The LSA algorithm constructs a document-term matrix (rows=documents, columns=words, cells=occurrence) and then applies Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to reduce dimensionality and encode documents with latent topic features.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe that LSA first builds a document-term matrix and then uses SVD to obtain low-dimensional topic representations.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These two candidates detail the two sequential main steps of the LSA algorithm, which together form a single procedural concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Entity-Level Sentiment Analysis on the Twitter Dataset
reconciled_candidates.description: Entity-level sentiment analysis judges sentiment (positive, negative, neutral) toward a specific entity in a text. The Twitter Entity Sentiment Analysis dataset provides multi-lingual tweets for this task, with irrelevant messages treated as neutral.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain what entity-level sentiment analysis is, list the three sentiment classes, and identify the Twitter dataset as a resource for this task.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates together define the entity-level task, its classes, and the specific dataset, forming a cohesive introduction to the sentiment analysis case study.

reconciled_candidates.label: Twitter Dataset Organization and License
reconciled_candidates.description: The dataset is split into training (twitter_training.csv) and validation (twitter_validation.csv) sets, evaluated using top-1 classification accuracy, and released under CC0 Public Domain license.
coverage_criteria: Student can state the dataset split files, the evaluation metric, and the license type.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These two candidates cover practical details about the dataset's usage and permissions, which are minor standalone facts best combined.
